title: Caring: A Relational Approach to Ethics and Moral Education
notes: First published 1984 with the subtitle 'A Feminine Approach to Ethics and Moral Education'. The 2013 updated edition adds a new preface and afterword. Place: Berkeley. Checked at: https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1525/9780520957343/html
about: Noddings grounds ethics in the caring relation between a 'one-caring' and a 'cared-for' rather than in universal principles. Caring requires engrossment (receptive attention to the other's reality) and motivational displacement toward the other's projects, and it is completed only when the cared-for receives and responds to the care. Moral education should therefore nurture the ethical ideal of caring rather than teach abstract reasoning.

title: The Ethics of Care: Personal, Political, and Global
notes: Place: Oxford; New York. One review dates the book 2005; most catalogue records give 2006. Checked at: https://ndpr.nd.edu/news/the-ethics-of-care-personal-political-global/
about: Held presents the ethics of care as a distinct moral theory, an alternative to Kantian and utilitarian ethics, that takes relations of care and interdependence rather than independent individuals as basic. She argues that care is both a practice and a value, and that its values should shape social and political institutions beyond the family. She extends the approach to the limits of rights-based and market thinking and to global civil society.

title: Moral Boundaries: A Political Argument for an Ethic of Care
notes: Place: New York. Checked at: https://www.routledge.com/Moral-Boundaries-A-Political-Argument-for-an-Ethic-of-Care/Tronto/p/book/9780415906425
about: Tronto argues that treating care as 'women's morality' is empirically and historically inaccurate and politically unwise, and that the boundaries separating morality from politics keep care marginal and protect the privileged. She defines care broadly as activity to maintain, continue and repair our world, and distinguishes four phases (caring about, taking care of, care-giving, care-receiving) with corresponding moral elements: attentiveness, responsibility, competence and responsiveness.

title: Caring Democracy: Markets, Equality, and Justice
notes: Place: New York. Checked at: https://experts.umn.edu/en/publications/caring-democracy-markets-equality-and-justice/
about: Tronto argues that democratic societies face a 'caring deficit' and that democracy should be rethought from a caring perspective, making the allocation of caring responsibilities, rather than economics, the central concern of democratic politics. She questions whether markets can be caring and proposes 'caring with' as a democratic ideal of shared responsibility.

title: Love's Labor: Essays on Women, Equality and Dependency
notes: First edition Routledge 1999. Second edition: Routledge gives copyright 2020 (BnF record: New York, Routledge, 2020); one bookseller lists 2019. Adds updated material on care workers, her disabled daughter and welfare reform. Checked at: https://www.routledge.com/Loves-Labor-Essays-on-Women-Equality-and-Dependency/Kittay/p/book/9781138089914
about: Kittay argues that liberal equality, modelled on independent and equally situated citizens, ignores the inevitable dependency of human life and the 'dependency workers' who meet it. Because dependency workers become vulnerable themselves, justice requires a principle of social responsibility for care (which she calls doulia) that supports those who care for dependants. She draws on her experience of caring for her severely disabled daughter.

title: In a Different Voice: Psychological Theory and Women's Development
notes: Place: Cambridge, MA. Later reissues exist (e.g. with a 1993 preface); cite the printing actually used. Checked at: https://librarycatalog.ecu.edu/catalog/188602
about: Gilligan argues that developmental psychology, especially Kohlberg's stage theory, misread women's moral reasoning by measuring it against a male-normed standard of justice and rights. Drawing on interview studies, she identifies a 'different voice' oriented to care, responsibility and relationships, which she presents as a distinct moral orientation rather than a deficient stage.

title: The Sovereignty of Good
notes: Series: Studies in Ethics and the Philosophy of Religion (ed. D. Z. Phillips). Three essays: 'The Idea of Perfection', 'On "God" and "Good"', 'The Sovereignty of Good over Other Concepts'. Reissued Routledge Classics 2001 (UNCONFIRMED: single bookseller source) and Routledge 2013 with a foreword by Mary Midgley (ISBN 9780415854733). Checked at: https://resolve.cambridge.org/core/journals/philosophy/article/sovereignty-of-good-by-iris-murdoch-routledge-and-kegan-paul-1970-140-paperback-70p/3E453F99B28779A1AB5D5469B656027D
about: Murdoch criticises the existentialist and analytic picture of the moral agent as a will choosing in isolated moments, arguing that moral life goes on continuously in how we see. Borrowing from Weil, she holds that 'attention', a just and loving gaze directed upon an individual reality, is the characteristic mark of the active moral agent; her example of a mother-in-law (M) who comes to see her daughter-in-law (D) more justly shows moral progress as inner reorientation. The Good, like art, draws us out of the 'fat relentless ego' toward reality.

title: Waiting for God
notes: Translated by Emma Craufurd; introduction by Leslie A. Fiedler. Translation of 'Attente de Dieu' (1950). Key essay: 'Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies with a View to the Love of God'. UNCONFIRMED: the Putnam imprint rests on a CiNii listing ('G.P. Putnam, c1951'); widely available reprints are Harper & Row (Harper Colophon, 1973) and HarperPerennial Modern Classics (2009), which carry the 1951 copyright. Cite the edition actually consulted. Checked at: https://ci.nii.ac.jp/author/DA03472899
about: A collection of Weil's letters and essays written to Father Joseph-Marie Perrin and others. In the school-studies essay she argues that the real purpose of study is to develop the faculty of attention, a waiting, receptive suspension of one's own thought, which is the substance of prayer and of love of neighbour; the capacity to give attention to someone who is suffering, to ask 'What are you going through?', is rare and precious.

title: Women and Human Development: The Capabilities Approach
notes: The Seeley Lectures, no. 3. Place: Cambridge. Checked at: https://chicagounbound.uchicago.edu/books/291/
about: Nussbaum develops a philosophical version of the capabilities approach, building on Sen, and defends a list of central human capabilities as universal norms that every government should secure to a threshold for each person. Focusing on poor women in India, she argues that gender inequality is a problem of justice and answers objections from cultural relativism and from the value of preferences, which can be adapted to injustice.

title: Creating Capabilities: The Human Development Approach
publisher: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press
notes: Place: Cambridge, MA. Checked at: https://search.worldcat.org/title/Creating-capabilities-:-the-human-development-approach/oclc/753976782
about: An accessible primer on the capabilities approach, which assesses human development by what people are actually able to do and to be rather than by GDP or utility. Nussbaum sets out her list of ten central capabilities (including life, bodily health, bodily integrity, practical reason, affiliation and play), argues that a just society must secure each to a threshold for every person as a matter of human dignity, and distinguishes her version from Sen's.

title: Development as Freedom
notes: Also published in the USA by Alfred A. Knopf, 1999 (the Oxford edition notes first US publication by Knopf). Based on lectures given at the World Bank in 1996-97. Checked at: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Development_as_Freedom
about: Sen argues that development should be understood as the expansion of the real freedoms people enjoy, their capabilities to lead lives they have reason to value, rather than as growth in income alone. Freedom is both the primary end and a principal means of development, with political freedoms, economic facilities, social opportunities, transparency guarantees and protective security reinforcing one another.

authors: Gold, Andrew S.; Miller, Paul B. (eds.)
title: Philosophical Foundations of Fiduciary Law
notes: Editors (eds.), not authors. Series: Philosophical Foundations of Law. Print ISBN 9780198701729. Checked at: https://scholarship.law.nd.edu/law_books/455
about: An edited collection of essays by legal philosophers and private-law theorists on the nature of fiduciary relationships, the content and justification of fiduciary loyalty, the relationship between fiduciary duties and morality, economic analyses of fiduciary law, and its extension to public and international law. The editors present it as setting an agenda for the philosophical study of fiduciary law.

title: Fiduciary Law
notes: Place: Oxford; New York. Catalogues give c2011; some listings (incl. BU repository) give 2010. ISBN 9780195391565. Checked at: https://wildy.com/isbn/9780195391565/fiduciary-law-hardback-oxford-university-press-usa
about: A comprehensive treatment of the structure, principles and objectives of fiduciary law across relationships in which property or power is entrusted to another, including corporate managers, money managers, lawyers and physicians. Frankel argues that entrustment and the resulting risk to the entrustor explain the duties of loyalty and care and the strictness with which law polices fiduciaries.

title: Fiduciary Law
notes: May 1983. First page 795 verified. UNCONFIRMED: end page (commonly given as 836) not verified.
about: Frankel's foundational article argues that fiduciary relationships form a distinct legal category, growing in importance in a society of specialised services, and that they share a common structure: the fiduciary is entrusted with power over the entrustor's property or interests for the entrustor's benefit. The entrustor's resulting vulnerability to abuse of that power justifies the special duties and remedies of fiduciary law.

title: The Critical Resource Theory of Fiduciary Duty
notes: UNCONFIRMED first page: the Vanderbilt repository's recommended citation gives 55 Vand. L. Rev. 1397, while BYU, SSRN-based and other citations give 1399. Check the printed volume.
about: Smith proposes a unifying theory of fiduciary law: a fiduciary relationship exists when one party acts on behalf of another while exercising discretion over a critical resource belonging to the beneficiary. Drawing on the property-rights theory of the firm, he argues that the core purpose of fiduciary duty is to combat opportunism in such relationships, which also explains why fiduciary duty is a close cousin of the contractual duty of good faith and why restitution is the usual remedy.

title: A Theory of Fiduciary Liability
about: Miller argues that fiduciary law lacks a coherent foundation and offers one drawn from the common law, starting from the Supreme Court of Canada's decision in Galambos v. Perez. The fiduciary relationship is a distinctive legal relationship in which one party holds discretionary power over the practical interests of another, and fiduciary duties can be explained entirely by the normatively significant features of that relationship.

title: Ethics for Adversaries: The Morality of Roles in Public and Professional Life
notes: Place: Princeton, NJ. Paperback 2000. Checked at: https://press.princeton.edu/books/ebook/9781400822935/ethics-for-adversaries-0
about: Applbaum examines the arguments professionals and officials use to justify acts in their roles that would be wrong if done by anyone else, opening with Sanson, the executioner of Paris who served successive regimes. He argues that appeals to fair play, consent and institutional authority are weaker than they appear, and that roles and institutions generally cannot create moral permissions to do what would otherwise be wrong.

title: Professional Ethics
notes: Place: Belmont, CA. Wadsworth Series in Social Philosophy. A 2nd edition (Wadsworth, 1989, ISBN 0534095461) is recorded in a single catalogue (relbib.de). Checked at: https://librarycatalog.ecu.edu/catalog/305305
about: A systematic treatment of the ethics of the professions in a liberal society. Bayles analyses the professional-client relationship through competing models (agency, contract, friendship, paternalism and his preferred fiduciary model, in which the professional has superior knowledge but the client retains significant authority over decisions) and sets out the obligations professionals owe to clients and to third parties, including honesty, candour, competence, diligence, loyalty, fairness and discretion.

title: The Lawyer as Friend: The Moral Foundations of the Lawyer-Client Relation
notes: Cited as 85 Yale L.J. 1060 (1976); July 1976. UNCONFIRMED: issue number (likely 8) and end page (commonly 1089) not verified.
about: Fried asks whether a good lawyer can be a good person, given the duty of partisan loyalty to clients. He answers by analogy with friendship: as a friend may legitimately prefer a friend's interests, the lawyer is a 'limited-purpose friend' who adopts the client's interests as their own within the legal system, which is justified because it serves the client's autonomy in dealing with the law.

title: Lawyers as Professionals: Some Moral Issues
notes: Journal of the ABA Section of Individual Rights and Responsibilities. Issue number not verified.
about: Often credited with inaugurating modern philosophical legal ethics, the article raises two criticisms of lawyers as professionals: role-differentiated behaviour leads lawyers to act amorally on behalf of clients, and the lawyer-client relationship is paternalistic and tends toward the lawyer's domination of the client. Wasserstrom locates the core of the problem in professionalism itself.

title: Trust and Antitrust
about: Baier argues that moral philosophy, preoccupied with contracts between equals, has neglected trust, especially between unequals. She analyses trust as accepted vulnerability to another's possible but not expected ill will toward something one cares about that is entrusted to them, and proposes a test of a trust relationship's moral decency: whether it could survive each party's knowledge of what the other relies on to sustain it.

title: Trust as an Affective Attitude
notes: UNCONFIRMED: DOI not verified. Volume, issue and pages confirmed via PhilArchive listings and a Cambridge course reading list.
about: Jones argues that trust is not mainly a belief but an affective attitude: optimism about another's goodwill and competence in the domain of interaction, together with the expectation that they will be directly and favourably moved by the thought that we are counting on them. The account explains why trust resists evidence and why betrayal provokes resentment rather than mere disappointment.

title: A Question of Trust: The BBC Reith Lectures 2002
notes: ISBN 9780521529969 (pbk), 9780521823043 (hbk). Checked at: https://openlibrary.org/books/OL7744799M
about: O'Neill questions the claim of a 'crisis of trust', noting that people continue to rely on the institutions they say they distrust. She argues that the audit and accountability culture adopted to restore trust often distorts professional practice and can undermine it, and that what is needed is intelligent accountability and communication that lets people assess trustworthiness; she also addresses deception and press freedom.

title: Autonomy and Trust in Bioethics
notes: The Gifford Lectures, University of Edinburgh, 2001. Checked at: https://cahss.ed.ac.uk/news-events/lectures/gifford-lectures/archive/archive-2000-2001/dr-oneill
about: O'Neill argues that the conceptions of individual autonomy dominant in bioethics are philosophically and ethically inadequate and tend to undermine rather than support trust between patients, professionals and institutions. She proposes instead a Kantian 'principled autonomy' and examines informed consent, genetic information, tissue research, reproductive technologies and medical reporting in the media.

title: Paternalism
notes: Widely reprinted. One older bibliography gives 1971; PhilPapers gives 1972.
about: Dworkin defines paternalism as interference with a person's liberty of action justified by reasons referring exclusively to that person's welfare, and distinguishes pure from impure paternalism. He argues that Mill's anti-paternalism combines a utilitarian argument, which supports only a presumption against interference, with an argument from the value of free choice, and he defends limited paternalism justified by what rational persons would consent to as 'social insurance'.

title: The Theory and Practice of Autonomy
notes: Cambridge Studies in Philosophy. Place: Cambridge; New York. Checked at: https://lib.ecu.edu/catalog-preview/catalog/330777
about: Dworkin develops a procedural, hierarchical account of autonomy as the capacity to reflect critically on one's first-order preferences and desires and to accept or change them in light of higher-order preferences. He then applies it to practical questions in applied ethics, including paternalism, informed and proxy consent in medicine, and entrapment by law-enforcement officials.

title: Relational Autonomy: Feminist Perspectives on Autonomy, Agency, and the Social Self
notes: Editors (eds.), not authors. Editors' introduction: 'Autonomy Refigured'. Place: New York. Checked at: https://academic.oup.com/book/49675
about: This collection rejects the claim that autonomy is inherently masculinist and instead 'refigures' it as relational, holding that persons are socially embedded and that their identities and capacities for agency are formed through social relationships. The contributors examine how oppressive socialisation can impair autonomy and bring feminist critiques to bear on debates about agency, identity and moral responsibility.

authors: Mackenzie, Catriona; Rogers, Wendy; Dodds, Susan (eds.)
title: Vulnerability: New Essays in Ethics and Feminist Philosophy
notes: Editors (eds.), not authors. Studies in Feminist Philosophy. Some listings give an online/copyright date of 2013; NDPR and the print paperback give 2014. Checked at: https://academic.oup.com/book/1543
about: The essays examine what vulnerability is, what responsibilities are owed to the vulnerable and by whom, and how responses to vulnerability can respect autonomy. The editors' introduction proposes a taxonomy distinguishing inherent, situational and pathogenic vulnerability (the last arising from morally dysfunctional relationships or institutions, including paternalistic responses), applied to disability, care, children, the elderly and intergenerational justice.

title: Protecting the Vulnerable: A Reanalysis of Our Social Responsibilities
notes: Place: Chicago. Checked at: https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/P/bo5974942.html
about: Goodin argues that our special responsibilities, to family, friends, clients and others, are grounded not in voluntary commitment but in the vulnerability of others to our actions and choices. Because the same principle reaches beyond those to whom we have committed ourselves, it also justifies wider social obligations, including the welfare state.

authors: Beauchamp, Tom L.; Childress, James F.
title: Principles of Biomedical Ethics
notes: First edition 1979. ISBN 9780190640873. Checked at: https://med.virginia.edu/biomedical-ethics/2019/11/22/40th-anniversary-and-8th-edition-of-principles-of-biomedical-ethics-by-jim-childress-and-tom-beauchamp/
about: The standard text of 'principlism' in biomedical ethics, organised around four prima facie principles: respect for autonomy, nonmaleficence, beneficence and justice, which are specified and balanced against one another in particular cases. It also treats professional-patient relationships, including veracity, privacy, confidentiality and fidelity, and the moral character of health professionals.
